study.title: Sampling: head versus tail
study.locator: Terminology (sampled versus not sampled); Head Sampling (decision from trace ID before the outcome); Tail Sampling (error and latency criteria; stateful operating cost)

focus: White-box metrics expose internals and imminent failure; black-box checks prove user-visible symptoms. Page on symptoms, debug with causes.

One label-value combination is one stored series. At \(3 \text{ services} \times 5 \text{ endpoints} \times 3 \text{ codes} \times 4 \text{ instances}\) the metric holds 180 series; adding a 200,000-value user label takes it to 9,000,000.
Head sampling decides from the trace ID before the outcome is known, so it cannot keep every error. Tail sampling waits for completed spans and pays stateful cost.
Keep what the Programming unit enforced: bounded label values, no secrets in attributes, and raw records retained behind every aggregate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the series count for labels service (3 values), endpoint (5), status (3) and instance (4): 180. Add user_id with 200,000 values: 9,000,000. State which label breaks the budget and give the bounded replacement: drop user_id from the metric and keep it on sampled traces only.
traps: Treating a shared request ID as proof of causation. Sampling, retries and shared queues break the causal reading; the ID joins evidence, it does not assign blame.
Putting request IDs, user IDs or tokens in metric labels. Each new value mints new series, and secrets in labels leak into every backend that stores them.
Averaging per-service p99 values and reading the result as the fleet p99. Merge histogram bucket counts or pool raw samples, then take the percentile.

selfTest.q: When should a page come from black-box rather than white-box monitoring?
selfTest.a: When the condition is already user-visible and urgent. White-box predicts or explains; black-box proves the symptom. Every page stays urgent, actionable and needing intelligence.

selfTest.q: A metric has labels with 3, 5, 3 and 4 values. How many series? What happens when a 200,000-value label is added?
selfTest.a: 180 series; then 9,000,000. Collection, storage and query cost scale with series count, so the unbounded label must move to sampled traces or logs.

selfTest.q: Why can head sampling miss every error in a release?
selfTest.a: Its decision uses the trace ID before the outcome exists. Keeping all errors needs tail sampling, which waits for completed spans and pays stateful cost.

selfTest.q: Two services report p99 values. Can you average them into a combined p99?
selfTest.a: No. The average of two quantiles is not the quantile of the pooled data. Merge their histograms or retained raw samples, with sample sizes, and compute it again.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the instrumented request path (request ID, queue wait, handler time, storage time, status, bounded labels) with local export, raw record retention and an enforced cardinality budget.

outcomes: Define latency, throughput, goodput, utilization and saturation, and separate queue wait from service time.
Report p50, p95 and p99 from raw samples with the sample size, and explain what the mean hides.
Measure a load sweep on your machine and name the saturated resource with its utilization.
units.why: Every SLO and capacity number later in this section reads a latency distribution. Assumed background: the Programming profiling-benchmarking unit, which built benchmark harnesses; this unit makes their output honest, with distributions first and one-number summaries never.

next.note: Turn the measured wait into concurrency and capacity math.
Rerun the sweep with an open-loop generator that cannot hide queueing.

study.title: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation
study.locator: The Four Golden Signals (latency of success versus failure; traffic; errors by policy; saturation with the 99th percentile over one minute as early signal)

study.title: Aggregation hides tails
study.locator: Aggregation (burst averaging example; percentile bands in Figure 4-1); A Note on Statistical Fallacies (mean versus median under skew)

study.title: Mean versus tail
study.locator: Worrying About Your Tail: 100 ms mean at 1,000 rps with 1% of requests at 5 seconds; exponential histogram buckets

study.title: Saturation and served-traffic metrics
study.locator: Metrics with Purpose (Saturation: track every resource, hard limits and degradation thresholds; Status of Served Traffic: break down by status and quota denial)

focus: Latency is a distribution. The SRE example (mean 100 ms, 1% at 5 s) and the Figure 4-1 bands show why one mean plus one threshold cannot describe user experience.

Goodput counts useful completions; throughput counts all completions; errors by policy can turn slow successes into failures. Saturation is the fraction of the most constrained resource, and most systems degrade before 100%.
Separate service time from queue wait in every measurement. Utilization explains which one dominates.
Percentiles need raw samples and \(n\). Report \(n\) with the value, never a bare p99.
units.reproduce: With CPython 3.14.4's random module and random.seed(7), draw 5000 samples: if random.random() < 0.02 take max(1, random.gauss(400, 80)), else max(1, random.gauss(40, 8)), in ms. With nearest-rank percentiles (rank \(\operatorname{ceil}(p \times n / 100)\)) you should get mean 48.19 ms, p50 40.16 ms, p95 55.16 ms, p99 421.05 ms and max 627.33 ms. Count the samples above 200 ms (108) and above 400 ms (60), and explain why a dashboard showing mean 48 ms and p95 55 ms shows none of them.
traps: Averaging percentiles from shards or windows. Shards with different traffic and tails give an average of p99s that is no request population's p99; pool the samples or merge histogram counts first.
Mixing failed-request latency into success latency, or dropping it. Fast 500s flatter the mean while slow errors are worse than fast ones; track both.
Reading 60% average utilization as headroom. The saturated resource is the most constrained one; queue wait grows on its utilization, not the average.

selfTest.q: In that run, mean is 48 ms and p95 is 55 ms over 5000 requests. How many requests are slower than 200 ms?
selfTest.a: 108, about 2%, and 60 of them are above 400 ms. Only the p99 (421 ms) hints at them. Count from the samples; the mean and p95 cannot tell you.

selfTest.q: Clients send 100 new requests/s. 10% fail on the first try and are retried once, and every retry succeeds. Offered load, throughput and goodput?
selfTest.a: Offered load and throughput are 110 attempts/s (100 successes plus 10 failures); goodput is 100 successful requests/s. Retries add 10% load without adding goodput.

selfTest.q: Utilization reads 85% but latency is flat. Saturated?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily. Saturation is about the most constrained resource and its queue. Check queue wait, queue depth, the 99th percentile trend and per-resource utilization.

selfTest.q: Why exponential histogram buckets?
selfTest.a: Latency spans orders of magnitude. Buckets growing by about 3x (0-10, 10-30, 30-100, 100-300 ms) resolve both the 40 ms body and the 400 ms tail without storing every sample.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a load sweep through saturation on the learner's service reporting p50, p95 and p99 from retained raw samples with \(n\), plus throughput, goodput, queue depth, utilization, errors and recovery.
units.stopWhen: Your script prints the five stated numbers, and you can explain the hidden 2% tail and name the saturation signal you would alert on.

study.title: Burn-rate alert shapes
study.locator: Ways to Alert on Significant Events (Alert on Burn Rate; Multiwindow, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerts)
study.depth: Read for alert-shape vocabulary only. Alert implementation belongs to the incidents unit.

focus: SLI is good events over total events; SLO is the target; the error budget is 100% minus the SLO times the window event count.
A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows 43.2 minutes of full outage; over 3 million requests it allows 3,000 errors. The same budget reads both ways.
Series availability multiplies (\(0.999 \times 0.995 = 0.99401\)) only for independent failures. Shared power, zones or deploys break the multiplication.
RPO bounds data loss (backup freshness); RTO bounds downtime (restore plus failover). MTBF 720 h with MTTR 1 h gives 0.99861, and holding 0.999 needs MTTR at most 0.72072 h.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the 30-day 99.9% budget (\(30 \times 24 \times 60 \times 0.001 = 43.2\) minutes), the series product \(0.999 \times 0.995 = 0.99401\) with independence stated, and the MTBF/MTTR pair \(720/721 = 0.99861\) with maximum MTTR \(720 \times 0.001/0.999 = 0.72072\) h. Then state the RPO check a restore drill must pass: the newest restorable record is no older than the RPO.
traps: A 100% SLO. Change itself is the top outage source, so 100% forbids deploys and leaves no room to improve.
Setting the SLO from current performance. It locks in heroic effort or hides user pain; start loose and tighten with evidence.
Quoting availability without the window and without independence. 99.9% over a week is 10.1 minutes, not 43.2.

selfTest.q: 3 million requests in 4 weeks at 99.9% availability: budget? One outage caused 1500 errors: share?
selfTest.a: 3,000 errors; the outage spent 50% of the budget.

selfTest.q: Two replicas at 0.99 each share one rack power feed. Combined availability?
selfTest.a: Not 0.9999. Parallel math assumes independent failures; the shared feed fails both at once, so the pair is no better than the feed itself.

selfTest.q: RPO is 1 hour and the last verified backup is 90 minutes old. Pass?
selfTest.a: No. Freshness exceeds RPO, so restore would lose up to 90 minutes. Take and verify a new backup.

selfTest.q: A burn-rate alert fires while the window SLO dashboard is green. What does that mean?
selfTest.a: Budget is being consumed fast relative to the window. The multiwindow alert predicts exhaustion before the window average moves.

units.title: Little's Law, capacity and queueing approximations
outcomes: State Little's Law with units and its stability assumption, and solve for any one of arrival rate, concurrency and time in system.
Derive capacity, utilization and headroom for requests, bytes, storage, memory and bandwidth from a stated workload.
Apply an M/M/1 or M/D/1 approximation with its assumptions written down, and report the uncertainty range.
units.why: Admission bounds and queue sizes from the Programming backpressure-graceful-shutdown unit, taken as assumed background, need numbers. This unit derives them: arrival rate times time in system is the queue you must bound.

next.note: Check the prediction by driving load through the knee.

study.title: M/M/1 stability and closed forms
study.locator: Model definition (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, single server, infinite buffer, FIFO); Stationary analysis (stability \(\lambda < \mu\), \(\rho = \lambda/\mu\)); Average number of customers in the system (\(L = \rho/(1 - \rho)\)); Response time (\(W = 1/(\mu - \lambda)\) via Little's Law)
study.depth: Use the closed forms as approximations only. Your service is not proven Poisson or exponential; the simulation in Reproduce is the check.

study.title: Capacity in resources, not queries
study.locator: The Pitfalls of 'Queries per Second' (cost per request varies; model capacity directly in CPU time and memory)

study.title: Conservative capacity and scaling bounds
study.locator: Autoscaling (Configuring Conservatively: stay far from bottlenecks, spare capacity for overload and redundancy; Setting Constraints: minimum and maximum bounds); Avoiding Overloading Backends

focus: \(L = \lambda W\) needs matching units: \((\text{requests}/\text{s}) \times \text{s} = \text{requests}\). It holds for long-run averages in a stable system; it predicts nothing about tails.

Utilization \(\rho = \lambda/\mu\) governs the wait. At \(\rho\) 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95 the M/D/1 mean wait is 0.5x, 2x and 9.5x the service time; a seeded 60 s simulation at 10 ms service measured 4.86, 19.97 and 80.87 ms against theory 5, 20 and 95 ms.
Capacity is per resource. The bottleneck is the smallest capacity-over-work ratio: \(12000/1\), \(5000/2\) and \(20000/0.5\) give 2500 rps at the database.
Approximations carry ranges. M/M/1 assumes Poisson arrivals and exponential service; burstier arrivals or heavier-tailed service widen the real wait. Report the assumption beside the number.
units.reproduce: Simulate a single FIFO server with CPython 3.14.4: random.seed(11), Poisson arrivals at 80/s from random.expovariate for 60 s, deterministic 10 ms service. The mean queue wait should be 20.475 ms against M/D/1 theory \(\rho \times S / (2 \times (1 - \rho)) = 20.000\) ms, so the mean time in system is 30.475 ms and Little's Law gives \(L = 80 \times 0.030475 = 2.44\). Check the law directly: the time-average number in system over 5 to 55 s is 2.52, against \(\lambda W\) 2.49 for the arrivals in that window. Then size servers: 0.8 average busy, so one server runs at \(\rho\) 0.8 and two at 0.4.
traps: Applying \(L = \lambda W\) to percentiles or to a draining queue. It relates long-run averages in a stable system only.
Quoting \(\lambda\) without a window. Poisson bursts exceed the average; size the bound for the peak window, not the daily mean.
Treating the M/M/1 number as measured. It is a prediction under strong assumptions; the simulation or load run is the check.

selfTest.q: 100 rps with 50 ms in system: average concurrency?
selfTest.a: 5 requests (\(100 \times 0.05\)). Units: \((\text{requests}/\text{s}) \times \text{s} = \text{requests}\).

selfTest.q: Single server at \(\rho\) 0.95: mean wait as a multiple of service time?
selfTest.a: M/D/1 gives \(\rho/(2 \times (1 - \rho)) = 9.5\)x; M/M/1 gives \(\rho/(1 - \rho) = 19\)x. State which model you used.

selfTest.q: Capacities \(12000/1\), \(5000/2\) and \(20000/0.5\) per request: max throughput and bottleneck?
selfTest.a: 2500 rps at the database (\(5000/2\)), the smallest ratio.

selfTest.q: The simulation gives 80.87 ms at \(\rho\) 0.95 against theory 95 ms. Contradiction?
selfTest.a: No. Near \(\rho\) 1 the queue relaxes slowly and the run starts empty, so a 60 s run reads low. Lengthen it, drop a warm-up, repeat with several seeds and report the spread beside the theory.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Solve Little's Law
practice.locator: LittlesLawCalculator.solve: detect the -1 argument and rearrange \(L = \lambda W\), rounded to 5 places (examples: \(100 \text{ rps} \times 0.05 \text{ s} = 5\); \(5/0.05 = 100\) rps)
practice.note: Attempt only after your own three-way derivations. Keep units attached: throughput in requests/s, latency in seconds.

study.title: Queue signals of saturation
study.locator: The Four Golden Signals (Saturation: 99th percentile over one minute as early signal); Choosing an Appropriate Resolution for Measurements

focus: Open-loop sends on a schedule whether or not replies returned; closed-loop waits for each reply. Past the knee, closed-loop self-throttles and reports flat latency while the queue explodes.

Seeded simulation (CPython 3.14.4, seed 21, 10 ms service, 500 ms stall every 200th request, 30 s): capacity is about 80.3 rps. Open loop at 60, 80 and 90 rps gives mean 96.3, 341.1 and 1843.1 ms and p99 502.8, 759.1 and 3727.5 ms, and the 90 rps numbers keep growing with run length. Closed loop with 5 clients gives mean 62.1 ms at 80.5 completed rps. Same server, different stories.
The first saturation point is where queue wait passes service time and goodput stops rising with offered load. Past it the bottleneck migrates: server CPU, then queue memory, then the dependency.
Keep every raw sample. Percentiles come from the retained records with \(n\); the generator log is part of the evidence.
units.reproduce: Write a small open-loop generator with CPython 3.14.4 (random.seed(21), Poisson schedule via random.expovariate, latency counted from the intended send time, one FIFO server with 10 ms service and a 500 ms stall on every 200th request, 30 s) and confirm the 80 rps row: mean 341.1 ms, p50 341.1 ms, p95 649.5 ms, p99 759.1 ms with nearest-rank percentiles. Then run the closed-loop twin (5 clients, next request on completion: mean 62.1 ms, p99 540.0 ms, 80.5 completed rps) and state which run to trust for tail latency and why.
traps: Tuning the closed loop until latency looks good. Fewer clients or think time hides the queue; the offered load is no longer the stated load.
Reading server-side latency only. Queue wait before the handler is user-visible latency; instrument arrival-to-start separately.
Calling the knee at 100% CPU. The first bottleneck is whatever queue grows first: threads, connections, memory or the dependency.

selfTest.q: Open-loop p99 is 759 ms and closed-loop p99 is 540 ms on the same server. Which is honest?
selfTest.a: Open-loop. Closed-loop skips the requests it never sent; the missing samples are the omitted coordination.

selfTest.q: Throughput rises with offered load, then flattens while p95 climbs. What happened?
selfTest.a: First saturation: the bottleneck server reached \(\rho\) near 1. Extra offered load becomes queue wait and errors, not completions.

selfTest.q: Why record intended send time, not just start and end?
selfTest.a: A request that should have gone out earlier was already waiting from the user's point of view. Measuring from the intended send time keeps that wait; measuring from the actual send drops it.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: an open-loop sweep of the learner's service through the predicted knee with retained raw records, measured p50, p95 and p99 with \(n\), queue depth, utilization, errors and recovery, reconciled against the Little's Law prediction.

study.title: Throttling, quotas and overload errors
study.locator: Per-Customer Limits; Client-Side Throttling (adaptive throttling, \(\text{requests} = 2 \times \text{accepts}\) cutoff, local rejection); Criticality; Utilization Signals; Handling Overload Errors (Deciding to Retry)

study.title: Shedding, retries and deadlines
study.locator: Queue Management; Load Shedding and Graceful Degradation; Retries; Latency and Deadlines (Picking a deadline; Deadline propagation; Cancellation propagation; Bimodal latency)

study.title: Slow starts and cascading tests
study.locator: Slow Startup and Cold Caching; Testing for Cascading Failures (Test Until Failure and Beyond)
study.depth: Read once for vocabulary. The fault harness itself runs in the incidents unit.

focus: Retries multiply per layer: 2 retries at each of 3 layers turn 1 user request into at most 27 backend attempts. Budgets cap attempts per request or per window, with jitter to de-synchronize them.

Adaptive throttling decides at the client from local accept and reject history (cutoff at \(\text{requests} = 2 \times \text{accepts}\)); per-customer quotas keep one bad customer from spending the whole backend.
Shed early and cheaply: reject above the bound before doing work, serve degraded answers while possible, and propagate deadlines plus cancellation so shed work actually stops.
Bimodal latency (fast rejects mixed with slow successes) is the signature of a shedding or partially overloaded path. Average it and you see neither mode.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the 27x worst case above (\((1 + 2)^3\)). Then set a budget for a service at 1000 rps that caps retries at 5% of requests (50 retry rps) with per-customer shares, and state where the breaker opens (client, server, or both) and what the fallback serves.
traps: Retrying on a saturated server. The retry adds queue wait for everyone; back off with jitter and count retries against the budget.
Shedding at the server only. Rejected requests still cost parsing, TLS and queue; client-side throttling stops them before the wire.
A deadline without propagation. Each layer waits out its own timeout, and the user waits for the sum.

selfTest.q: 3 layers with 1 retry each: worst-case attempts per user request?
selfTest.a: 8 (\(2^3\)). Retries compose multiplicatively across layers.

selfTest.q: The backend spends as much CPU rejecting as serving. What changes?
selfTest.a: Lower the adaptive multiplier toward 1.1 and throttle at the client. Server-side rejection alone still overloads the backend.

selfTest.q: p50 falls while p99 climbs during overload. Explain.
selfTest.a: Bimodal path: cheap rejects pull the median down while queued successes stretch the tail. Report both modes, not the mean.

selfTest.q: When is a degraded answer better than an error?
selfTest.a: When it is cheaper to compute and still useful (stale copy, partial corpus). Under extreme overload, shed to errors rather than collapse.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: bounded admission, a per-customer retry budget with jitter, client-side throttle, a breaker with fallback, and propagated deadlines with cancellation in the learner's service slice, each demonstrated under injected overload.
units.stopWhen: You derive the 27x case and defend one budget (rate, shares, breaker placement, fallback) against a retry storm you inject.

fit.note: SRE overload and cascading-failure chapters cover budgets, throttling, shedding and deadlines at explain and derive depth; overload behavior is practised in the mini-project.

units.title: Failure domains, correctness signals and safe rollout
outcomes: Map replicas to failure domains and name the single points the replica count hides.
Walk two simultaneous failures and state preserved and violated invariants.
Run a canary with population, duration, representative metrics and rollback rule, and read its result.
Separate health and readiness from domain-specific correctness signals.
units.why: Container readiness, liveness and SIGTERM drains from the Programming health-containers-runbooks unit, taken as assumed background, tell you a process runs. This unit asks whether it serves correctly, and whether one rollout or one zone loss takes everything with it.

next.note: Work the timeline when the canary fails.
Reason about ordering under the same partitions.

study.locator: Requirements of a Canary Process; Choosing a Canary Population and Duration; Selecting and Evaluating Metrics (Metrics Should Indicate Problems; Metrics Should Be Representative and Attributable; Before/After Evaluation Is Risky); Requirements on Monitoring Data (split canary from control; metric intervals within canary duration)

study.locator: Dependencies and Isolation (shared backends couple canary and control; check absolute SLOs); Use a Gradual Canary for Better Metric Selection; Related Concepts (Blue/Green Deployment)

study.title: What triggers cascading failure
study.locator: Triggering Conditions for Cascading Failures (Process Death; Process Updates; New Rollouts; Organic Growth); Testing for Cascading Failures (Test Until Failure and Beyond)

focus: Replicas in one zone are one failure. API across two zones survives; a database with both copies in us-east-1a does not. Count zones per component, not replicas.
Safe quorums need \(R + W > N\) and \(2 \times W > N\). \(N=5\), \(R=3\), \(W=3\) holds; \(N=4\), \(R=2\), \(W=2\) lets two disjoint halves both take writes.

Canary metrics must indicate user-visible problems and attribute to the change: reuse SLIs, prefer crash and failure signals in the small first stage, split canary from control in monitoring, and distrust before/after comparisons across time.

Health says the process answers; correctness signals say the answers are right. A serving-but-wrong version passes readiness and needs a domain check (output quality, freshness watermark, reconciliation count).
units.reproduce: Closed-book, map components api (zones a, b), db (a, a) and cache (c): at-risk components are db and cache (under two zones), and the dead set after zone a fails is db. Then take a five-replica store with \(N=5\), \(R=3\), \(W=3\) spread 2, 2 and 1 over zones a, b and c: walk zone-a loss plus a bad canary on 5% of traffic, and state what still serves reads and writes and what the canary metrics must show before rollback.
traps: Counting two replicas as redundancy. Same zone, same deploy, same config or same dependency is one domain.
Promoting a canary on aggregate error rate. A 5% canary at 20% errors reads as 1% overall; split canary versus control first.
Splitting blame evenly between canary and control. Shared backends couple them, so also check absolute SLOs, not just the A/B gap.

selfTest.q: db replicas live in a and a; cache has one copy in c. At-risk? Dead after a fails?
selfTest.a: At-risk: db and cache (each under two zones). Dead after a fails: db only.
No. \(R+W\) and \(2W\) equal \(N\) instead of exceeding it, so disjoint halves can both take writes.

selfTest.q: Canary errors are flat but p95 is up 10%. Promote?
selfTest.a: Not on error rate alone. Latency SLIs indicate user-visible harm; hold or roll back per the metric policy, then check attribution.

selfTest.q: Readiness passes but answers are wrong. What is missing?
selfTest.a: A domain correctness signal: sampled output checks, a freshness watermark or a reconciliation count, alerted like an SLI.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Audit Failure Domains
practice.locator: atRiskComponents (under two distinct zones) and unavailableAfter (every replica in the failed zone), sorted without duplicates
practice.note: Attempt only after your own zone map. Two replicas in one zone still share that zone.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Simulate Partition Quorums
practice.locator: partitionStatus (READ_WRITE, READ_ONLY, WRITE_ONLY, UNAVAILABLE) and hasSafeQuorums (\(R + W > N\) and \(2W > N\))
practice.note: Attempt only after your own quorum arithmetic. A reachable majority is not a safe quorum.

units.stopWhen: You map zones, quorums and canary result without notes and can state which simultaneous pair your design survives.

units.title: Backups, runbooks, incident timelines and postmortems
outcomes: Work a timeline from telemetry and state detection, diagnosis, mitigation and recovery times.
Execute a runbook for process death, dependency outage, bad rollout, corrupt state and overload, and verify restore against RPO and RTO.
Write a blameless postmortem with owned action items and one regression guard.
units.why: All earlier evidence pays off here. Assumed background: hypothesis-driven debugging from the Programming testing-debugging-reproducibility units. This unit turns it into team procedure: timelines, roles, runbooks and postmortems.

next.note: Price the prevention work the postmortem asks for.
Feed the measured budget loss back into targets.

study.locator: Triage; Examine (Logging); Diagnose (Simplify and reduce; Ask what, where and why); Test and Treat; Negative Results Are Magic

study.locator: Incident Management at Google (Incident Command System; Main Roles in Incident Response); Putting Best Practices into Practice (Prepare Beforehand; Drills)

study.locator: Bad Postmortem versus Good Postmortem (satellite diskerase: context, blamelessness, concrete action items with owners); Organizational Incentives (Reward action item closeout)

study.title: Disaster testing discipline
study.locator: Testing Disaster
study.depth: Read for restore-verification discipline only: backups count when a drill restores them inside RPO and RTO.

study.title: Runbook and artifact evidence
study.locator: Failure-injection requirements (worker crash and hang, corrupt partial run, incompatible resume); Measurement requirements (distributions, queue occupancy, failed and retried work); Milestone F (reviewer-seeded unseen failure diagnosed from artifacts); short runbook for interrupted, hung or corrupt runs

focus: Timelines carry times, not adjectives: detected at, diagnosed at, mitigated at, recovered at, plus measured RTO and RPO loss counted from the newest restorable record.
Runbooks are tested procedures with owners: one each for process death, dependency outage, bad rollout, corrupt state and capacity exhaustion, each ending in a verified restore.
Good postmortems are blameless, prompt and owned: context, mechanism, action items with owners and dates, and one regression guard that fails if the bug returns.
Negative results are evidence. A ruled-out cause with its test stays in the timeline so the next responder does not repeat it.
units.reproduce: Seed one fault in your service (kill a worker mid-run, corrupt one record, or deploy the bad version behind your canary split), work it with your runbook, and produce a timeline with detection, diagnosis, mitigation and recovery times, measured RTO and counted RPO loss, plus one merged regression test. There are no fixed numbers: yours are the evidence.
traps: Declaring recovery at mitigation. Recovery is verified restore plus SLO compliance over the window, not the moment the alert clears.
Writing the postmortem as verdict. Blame ends inquiry; mechanism plus owned actions prevent recurrence.
Trusting untested backups. An unverified backup is a hope; restore drills against RPO and RTO are the practice.

selfTest.q: The alert clears 10 minutes after the fix but p99 stays high for an hour. Recovered at 10 minutes?
selfTest.a: No. Recovery needs restored SLO compliance; the tail shows continued user impact or a second fault.

selfTest.q: Two responders each fixed something but the timeline shows one fix. Problem?
selfTest.a: Yes. The timeline must record every action with times, or the next incident repeats the hidden work and misattributes the cure.

selfTest.q: A restore drill recovers everything but the last 90 minutes with RPO 1 hour. Pass?
selfTest.a: No. Loss exceeds RPO; shorten the backup interval or narrow the loss window, then re-drill.

selfTest.q: Action item reads improve monitoring with no owner. Accept?
selfTest.a: No. Owned, dated and verifiable, plus a regression guard; otherwise it never closes.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: one injected incident worked end to end (timeline, runbook execution, verified restore with measured RTO and counted RPO loss), a blameless postmortem with owned actions, and one merged regression guard.
units.stopWhen: Your timeline, runbook run, restore drill and postmortem exist as artifacts, and the regression test fails on the re-seeded fault.

fit.note: SRE troubleshooting, workbook response and postmortem chapters with the kit runbook and artifact contract cover timelines, restore and postmortems at implement depth.

units.title: Unit cost, headroom and simpler designs
outcomes: Derive per-request unit cost in the constrained resource and the provisioned headroom for a stated workload.
Defend the design against a 10x workload change with numbers: scale, shed, degrade or simplify.
Compare against a simpler alternative and name what the complexity buys.
units.why: Reliability without cost is a wish. This unit turns the saturation and capacity numbers into a provisioning choice the team can afford, and keeps the simpler design on the table.

next.note: Carry SLO, capacity and cost reasoning to replicated designs.
Revisit targets once cost bounds what reliability can be bought.

study.title: Risk tolerance and the cost of reliability
study.locator: Risk Tolerance of Services (Target level of availability; Cost); Identifying the Risk Tolerance of Infrastructure Services

study.title: Spare capacity and scaling limits
study.locator: Autoscaling (Configuring Conservatively: spare capacity for overload and redundancy; Setting Constraints: minimum and maximum bounds, quota)

study.title: Simplicity defense
study.locator: Design-defense questions (When should this remain a script instead of this package)
study.depth: Use the one question as the simpler-alternative test for your design. The full kit returns in later stages.

focus: Unit cost is per useful request in the constrained resource: 10 ms service time is 0.01 CPU-s per request, so 80 rps costs 0.8 CPU and 95 goodput rps costs 0.95 CPU.
Headroom is provisioned over expected peak at a utilization target: 0.8 CPU at a 0.7 target provisions about 1.14 CPUs, with autoscale bounds and kill switches capping the bill when the model breaks.

10x (800 rps) is 8 CPU-seconds of work per second, so about 11.4 CPUs at the same 0.7 target, or shedding, degrading or removing work. Amdahl bounds splitting one request or job across CPUs: 90% parallel on 4 CPUs gives 3.08x, not 4x.
The simpler alternative (one process, no cache, fewer moving parts) wins unless the complex design names the failure or cost it removes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive from 10 ms service and 80 rps: 0.8 CPU used, about 1.14 CPUs provisioned at a 0.7 target. Show the 10x table (800 rps is 8 CPUs busy, about 11.4 provisioned at 0.7, or shed, degrade or simplify), and the Amdahl check for parallelizing one job: \(1/(0.1 + 0.9/4) = 3.07692\).
traps: Pricing peak capacity at 100% utilization. Queue math forbids it; buy the headroom or buy the queue.
Counting hosts instead of the constrained resource. Cost follows CPU-s, bytes stored and bytes moved per request, not box count.
Letting experiment capacity become permanent. Time-box canary and load-test capacity and remove it in the rollback plan.

selfTest.q: 80 rps at 10 ms service with target \(\rho\) 0.7: provision?
selfTest.a: \(0.8/0.7 = \text{about } 1.14\) CPUs. Round up to whole CPUs, set the autoscale minimum and bound the maximum.

selfTest.q: Amdahl with 0.9 parallel on 4 CPUs: speedup? What does it say about 10x load?
selfTest.a: 3.07692, and never above 10x with any CPU count. That caps speeding up one job. Serving 10x more independent requests needs 10x the CPU-seconds, or less work per request, shedding or degradation.

selfTest.q: A simpler single-process design handles 3x but not 10x. Keep the complex one?
selfTest.a: Only with numbers: name the load where simplicity breaks, price both, and show what the complexity removes (failure domain, cost or toil).

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Calculate Amdahl's Law Speedup
practice.locator: AmdahlSpeedupCalculator.speedup: 1/((1 - parallelFraction) + parallelFraction/processors), rounded to 5 places (examples: 0.9 on 4 gives 3.07692)
practice.note: Attempt only after your own serial-fraction estimate. Compare the platform answer with the scale-out limit in your 10x defense.

units.stopWhen: You derive unit cost, headroom and the 10x table without notes and can defend the simpler alternative against your design with numbers.
